prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, and for showing how selection into exporting and foreign investment and reallocation across firms shape aggregate productivity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single part on B010, credited to Melitz and Helpman. What round 1 changed is the wording and my confidence in the attribution. The case rests on one identifiable discovery. Melitz (2003) moved trade analysis from the industry to the firm, so exporter selection, within-industry reallocation and aggregate productivity effects of liberalisation follow from firm-level productivity differences. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and Helpman's wider firm-level work extend the same logic to foreign investment and the boundaries of the firm. The framework is more than twenty years old, has been tested on firm-level data in many countries, and is standard in teaching, empirical trade and policy evaluation. The chair's summary shows that the eight B010 supporters name the same pair. I use that as evidence that the attribution is stable across assessors, not as evidence of merit, and I note that I am one of the eight. On the chair's wording question, I propose a citation limited to firm heterogeneity, selection and reallocation, with no career-wide framing for Helpman. Its reference to foreign investment follows Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and is the one extension I would keep in the text. The Bernard-Jensen exporter facts, Eaton-Kortum, Hopenhayn and Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions would be acknowledged in the scientific background, not through the laureate set. I would also separate the qualitative result from the quantitative one. The selection and reallocation mechanism does not depend on a Pareto productivity distribution. The size of the welfare gains does depend on distributional and other structural assumptions. From my recollection, parts of the literature find that under some assumptions gains formulas look similar to those of representative-firm models, which is a caveat on magnitudes and not on the mechanism. The citation should therefore not promise a particular welfare number. Under the three-person cap no second part is feasible alongside B010. B019 with two names plus B010 would total four, and B003 would need three names. A single part is the cleanest configuration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains credit. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and Hopenhayn in firm dynamics, are real precursors or parallel contributors, and a two-name prize leaves them out. I accept this as a cost and not a technicality. A second reservation is that the quantitative gains-from-trade magnitudes are model-dependent, and some of the incremental welfare claims for heterogeneity beyond representative-firm models are contested. A third is field balance after the 2008 trade prize. I think the distinctness argument holds, but the Committee should test it. B019 has a cleaner single-mechanism story and two-author attribution, and members who weigh that more heavily than breadth of confirming evidence are making a defensible choice. I also cannot rule out that my own assessment is influenced by my macro and growth interest in how micro-level productivity differences aggregate. My assessments come from my own recollection of the literature and have not been independently verified.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B019 (Kiyotaki and Moore) as his preferred part. He now treats B010 as a serious alternative, but he points to the credit disputes with Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Eaton-Kortum, and to the fact that two-name parts of B010 and B019 cannot be combined under a three-person cap.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved on distinctness, and I accept your point that B019 has the tighter single-mechanism attribution. I do not think the B010 credit dispute is larger than the one in B019. For B019 the open questions are Gertler and Gilchrist and the overlap with the 2022 recognition. For B010 the precursors are acknowledged as parallel or motivating strands, but the unifying selection model is carried by Melitz with Helpman's extensions. We agree that two parts cannot be combined without breaking the three-name cap, so the choice is between two single-part proposals. The remaining difference between us is how to weigh a single clean mechanism against a much larger body of firm-level confirmation. I weigh the confirmation more heavily, and I do not claim that this settles the matter on merit.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B019 first with Kiyotaki and Moore, but says he is not fully settled on the order of B019 and B010. He regards B019 as a distinct mechanism from the 2022 work on banks and runs, and says B010's empirical record is more mature.
responses.response: I accept your distinction between the 2022 work on banks and runs and Kiyotaki-Moore's collateral and asset-price feedback in the real economy, and I withdraw any suggestion that the overlap is fatal. It remains a matter of thematic adjacency that the Committee must weigh. Narrowing to two names was the right call, and my own opening inclusion of Gertler is one I have withdrawn. Your acknowledgement that B010 has the more mature empirical record is where we differ on weight, not on facts. If the Committee finds that the direct evidence for the collateral channel is stronger than I recall, B019 would move up in my ordering, which is why it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B032 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that the causal evidence on adjustment costs has been stress-tested for a decade, that continued debate over magnitudes shows scrutiny and not fragility, and that B010 is her main alternative.
responses.response: I agree that debate over magnitudes is not in itself a sign of fragility, and I also agree that B032's causal designs are among the most transparent in the shortlist. My difficulty is the same one you identified, namely that the entry bundles two strands. Narrowing to the trade-shock core clarifies the laureate set, but then a good part of the technology-and-tasks story that motivates the broader prize is no longer being credited. The shift-share identification debate and the unsettled long-run welfare picture also affect how far a citation could go. That is why I rank B032 fifth. I would not put it above B010 or B019, but I do not regard your move to Dorn from Katz as a weak choice.

responses.point: Andersson moved B010 to first place and keeps B003 and B019 as alternatives. He treats B003 as scientifically strong but with narrower support and a harder boundary question over Bresnahan, Reiss and Benkard.
responses.response: I agree that the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes trio is the cleanest credit structure on B003, and I answer the chair's question by saying that I would not add Bresnahan, Reiss or Benkard to the core. A three-name BLP set is defensible on the demand-estimation contribution. But then the award would be best framed as a methods prize, and the Bresnahan omission would have to be handled in the background. I find that less secure than B010's attribution, which is why B003 is my second alternative and not my preferred part. I would reconsider only if the Committee decided that the methodological framing was the right one.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee accepts that the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum, Hopenhayn and Redding can be handled through the citation wording and the scientific background, and not through the laureate set.
How far the welfare-gain magnitudes survive alternative productivity distributions and structural assumptions, and whether that should change the wording of the citation.
Whether B010 is judged sufficiently distinct from the 2008 new-trade-theory prize, and how much weight field balance should have among the common criteria.
Whether the evidence for the collateral-amplification channel in B019 is stronger than I recall, and whether the overlap with the 2022 prize is judged decisive.
Whether the BLP-only trio for B003 would be accepted as a defensible methods award, given the Bresnahan boundary question.
My literature assessments rely on my own recollection and on colleagues' round-1 statements, and I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: As chair I disclose that I am one of the eight explicit B010 supporters, so my view should be read as one position within that group and not from outside it. My profile shows no tie to Helpman, Melitz, Kiyotaki, Moore, or the credited names on B003, and none of them is among my documented co-authors or institutional ties. I disclose collegial ties to committee members: IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart, co-author with Boppart on the epidemiological-economic paper, co-author with Friberg on the menu-costs paper (with Ellingsen), and a frequent co-author of Krusell. I also note that the 2018 Scientific Background cites my own 2014 work, which is not on this shortlist. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated, and I propose no recusals. My own research is in climate economics, macroeconomics and public finance, and not in the field of the preferred prize.
